warmup.q: The payments app logs a machine as fd00:10:6:0:0:0:0:10. Its list of machines allowed to send refunds has fd00:10:6::10, and the check, which compares the two as text, says they differ. Are they the same address?
options: No: the logged one has eight groups, so it's a longer address
Yes: :: stands for exactly the zero groups the log spells out
Only if both machines are on the same network
No: one of them is an IPv4 address in disguise
warmup.why: Every IPv6 address is 128 bits, however it's written. :: stands for a run of zero groups, here the four between 6 and 10, so both strings name the same 128 bits. Java's getHostAddress() prints the long form, which is why this mismatch is so common. Compare addresses as numbers, or turn both into the one standard spelling first (RFC 5952, in the first section).

sections.h: Writing a 128-bit address, and the one correct way to shorten it
sections.html:
Start with the address from the opening, fd00:10:6::10. It looks nothing like 10.10.1.10, and there's a reason. Every packet, the small piece of data a network carries, has a label with two IP addresses on it: where it's from and where it's going. IP addresses, subnets and NAT ended with the version in use today, IPv4, running out. An IPv4 address is 32 bits (binary digits), which gives about 4.3 billion addresses. IANA, the body that hands out blocks of addresses, gave away its last free blocks in 2011. Since then NAT has kept the internet going: a trick in which a router, the machine that passes packets between networks, hides a whole building behind one public address.

IPv6 (RFC 8200, the document that defines it) fixes the shortage by brute force. Its addresses are 128 bits, about 3.4 × 10^38 of them. That's enough to give every network on earth 2^64 addresses each (about 18 billion billion) and still not notice. It's not a future technology, either. Cloudflare is a company that carries a large share of the web's traffic. In 2025, it saw 29% of requests from machines that could use both versions arrive over IPv6, and 67% in India.

Writing 128 bits the IPv4 way, as numbers with dots between them, would take 16 numbers. So IPv6 writes eight groups of 16 bits in hex (base 16, with digits 0 to 9 and a to f), separated by colons:

fd00:0010:0006:0000:0000:0000:0000:0020

That's still long, so two shortening rules apply. Leading zeros in a group may go: 0010 becomes 10, and 0000 becomes 0. And one run of all-zero groups may be replaced by ::, which means "as many zero groups as it takes to make eight". The address above becomes fd00:10:6::20. That's the machine called api in the lab network. The lab network is a few pretend machines on your laptop, each a Docker container with its own network card, the part of a machine that joins it to a network. :: may appear only once. In 2001:db8::1::2, nobody could tell how many zeros belong on each side.

The rules are optional, and that's where the trouble starts. fd00:10:6::20, fd00:10:6:0::20, FD00:0010:6::0020 and fd00:10:6:0:0:0:0:20 are all the same address, the way "10 High Street" and "10 High St." are the same door. The last one is what Java prints: its Inet6Address.getHostAddress() drops leading zeros and never uses ::.

Any code that compares addresses as text then breaks. Think of a list of machines that are allowed in, or code that counts requests per address to stop one client from sending too many. Think of a search of the logs for one customer's requests, or a database (a program that stores records) told to hold each address once. Each one sees two spellings as two machines.

An address is a number, not a string. Parse it before you compare it. When you must print or store it as text, use one spelling. RFC 5952 picks that spelling, the canonical form, and every tool should print it:

  • lower-case hex, and no leading zeros in a group;
  • :: replaces the longest run of two or more zero groups, and the first such run if two are equally long;
  • a single zero group stays 0, never ::.

So 2001:db8:0:0:1:0:0:1 is 2001:db8::1:0:0:1, and 2001:db8:0:1:1:1:1:1 keeps its lone zero. The lab has you write this formatter, and its tests feed it what Java really prints.

Blocks of addresses use the same slash notation as IPv4. fd00:10:6::/64 means that the first 64 bits, the prefix, name the network, and the last 64 bits, the interface ID, name one network card inside it. Nearly every IPv6 network is a /64, because the way machines pick their own addresses (the third section) needs 64 bits for the interface ID. A company or a home gets a bigger block from its internet provider, often a /48 or a /56, and cuts /64s from it.

Now we can write an address. Next, let's look at one network card and count how many it has.

try.title: Read your IPv6 addresses
steps: From the labs folder, start the lab network if it isn't running: docker compose -f env/net.yml up -d. Its network called dual runs both versions of IP on one link. app has 10.10.6.10 and fd00:10:6::10, and api has 10.10.6.20 and fd00:10:6::20, with a web server (a program that hands out pages when asked) on port 8080.

Print app's IPv6 addresses. Before you run the Python lines, write two things by hand: the full eight-group form of fd00:10:6::10, and the canonical form of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:0001. Python's ipaddress module prints both (exploded is the full form, and compressed the short one).

On a Mac, ifconfig en0 | grep inet6 shows your Wi-Fi card's IPv6 addresses. If your network has IPv6, look for the words secured and temporary after the global ones: the stable random address and the daily one from the next section.

code.title: in labs/
code.html: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app ip -6 addr show eth0 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app python3 -c 'import ipaddress as i; a = i.ip_address("fd00:10:6::10"); print(a.exploded); print(a.compressed); print(i.ip_address("2001:0db8:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:0001"))'

try.expect:
From one run:

11: eth0@if534: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc noqueue state UP group default  link-netnsid 0
    inet6 fd00:10:6::10/64 scope global nodad
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
    inet6 fe80::10fc:1ff:fe3b:eb52/64 scope link
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
fd00:0010:0006:0000:0000:0000:0000:0010
fd00:10:6::10
2001:db8::1:0:0:1

There are two addresses on one card. The first is the one Docker gave it. It says scope global, although it's a unique local address, a private kind the next section explains, and nodad means Docker skipped the check for duplicates. The second, starting with fe80, is a link-local address the kernel, the core of the operating system, made itself. Yours will differ, because Docker gives the card a new random hardware address each time it starts. In the last line, two runs of two zero groups tie, so the first one becomes ::.

aside.title: If IPv6 fixes the shortage, why is IPv4 still everywhere?
aside.html: An IPv6-only machine can't talk to an IPv4-only machine directly, because their headers and addresses are different. So every machine, router and program on a path has to support IPv6 before traffic can use it, and there are billions of them. NAT made the shortage bearable, which took away the hurry. The result is a long time of both at once: most networks run the two side by side, which the last section calls dual stack.

sections.h: One card, several addresses, each good for a different distance
sections.html:
Look at app's card in the lab network and count its IPv6 addresses. There are two, and after the next section there will be three. In IPv4, a card normally has one address. In IPv6, several at once is the design. Each address has a scope: how far away it means anything. Think of "the flat upstairs", which works only inside your building, and a full postal address, which works anywhere.

The first bits of an address say which kind it is:

Prefix Kind Closest IPv4 kind
fe80::/10 link-local: valid on one link only 169.254.0.0/16
fc00::/7, in practice fd00::/8 unique local (ULA): private, never routed on the internet private blocks such as 10.0.0.0/8
2000::/3 global unicast: public, routed everywhere public addresses
::1 loopback: this machine 127.0.0.1
ff00::/8 multicast: one packet to every member of a group broadcast, roughly

A link is one stretch of network that machines share directly, with no router in between, like the lan in Routing, ICMP and traceroute. In IPv4, a broadcast is one packet that every card on the link receives. IPv6 has no broadcast at all. Multicast groups do its jobs instead: a card joins a group, and only members receive the packets sent to it. ff02::1 is every machine on the link, and ff02::2 is every router.

Two prefixes appear in examples. 2001:db8::/32 is set aside for documentation (RFC 3849), so it never belongs to a real network. And a real unique local prefix has 40 random bits after fd (RFC 4193). Then two companies that merge don't collide, the way two networks that both use 10.0.0.0/8 do. The lab's fd00:10:6::/64 skips the random part, to be easy to type.

Every IPv6 card has a link-local address, and the machine makes it itself before anyone sets anything up. Here's how app got fe80::10fc:1ff:fe3b:eb52 from its MAC address 12:fc:01:3b:eb:52. (A MAC address is the hardware address of a network card, six bytes long, from The link layer: Ethernet, MAC addresses and ARP.) Take the six bytes. Flip the U/L bit in the first byte, the bit that says whether the card's maker assigned the address, so 12 becomes 10. Put ff:fe in the middle. That gives the 64-bit interface ID 10fc:01ff:fe3b:eb52, and fe80:: goes in front. This recipe is called modified EUI-64 (RFC 4291), and the Linux kernel uses it by default.

It has a privacy problem. The same interface ID follows a laptop from network to network, so anyone watching can tell it's the same laptop. So macOS, Windows and phones use random interface IDs instead. They stay the same on one network (the idea of RFC 7217), and temporary addresses that change daily are used for connections going out (RFC 8981).

Link-local addresses come with one surprise. Every link uses the same fe80::/64, so a machine with two cards can't tell which one you mean. You must name the card, called the zone, after a %: fe80::e8cd:e9ff:fe43:37ae%eth0. Leave it out, and ping, the tool that sends a small "are you there?" message, warns you and gets no answer. Java keeps the zone as the scope ID of an Inet6Address.

Why bother with addresses that work on one link only? Because they exist before any other address does. Next, we'll watch a machine use them to find a router and build its global address.

try.title: Work out a link-local address, then ping it
steps: Print app's MAC address and IPv6 routes, and api's link-local address. Work out app's link-local address from its MAC by hand: flip the 0x02 bit of the first byte, and put ff:fe in the middle. Compare your answer with what ip -6 addr showed in the last Try it.
Copy api's fe80:: address into LL, and ping it twice: once without a zone, then with %eth0. Predict which one works.

Without %eth0, the kernel doesn't know which link the address belongs to, and ping even tells you so. Look at the routes too: fe80::/64 is on every IPv6 card, and Docker's gateway fd00:10:6::1 is the default router.

sections.h: A machine gives itself an address, and finds its neighbors without ARP
sections.html:
Where did app's addresses come from? Docker gave it fd00:10:6::10, and the kernel made the link-local one. On a real network, a machine has to get its address from somewhere. In IPv4, there are two ways. Someone types it in, or a DHCP server hands it out: a program on the network that lends addresses and keeps a table of who has which. IPv6 can use a DHCP server too, called DHCPv6. But its usual way needs no server and no table: SLAAC, stateless address autoconfiguration (RFC 4862). The machine builds its own address from a prefix that the router announces.

Let's build it up from the pieces we have. The machine already has a link-local address. Before it uses it, it checks that nobody else on the link has the same one. That check is called duplicate address detection. The machine sends a Neighbor Solicitation, "who has this address?", from the unspecified address ::, because it has no address of its own yet. If anyone answers, the address is taken.

Next, the machine needs a prefix that the rest of the world can reach, and only a router knows one. So the router multicasts a Router Advertisement to ff02::1, every machine on the link. It sends one every few minutes, and whenever a machine asks with a Router Solicitation. It says three things. This /64 is on this link. You may build your own address in it. And you may use me as your default router, the one to send everything else to, for 1,800 seconds.

The machine glues its interface ID behind the prefix, checks the new address the same way, and adds a default route through the router's link-local address. The router never learns which address the machine took. That's the "stateless" in SLAAC: nobody keeps a list. Picture a street where the council puts up a sign with the street's name. Each house picks its own number, shouts it once down the street to check that nobody else has it, and starts getting mail.

The same Neighbor Solicitation also replaces ARP. In The link layer: Ethernet, MAC addresses and ARP, an IPv4 machine used ARP to find the MAC address behind an IP address. It asked every card on the link at once. IPv6's version is called neighbor discovery (RFC 4861). Its messages are ICMPv6, IPv6's own messages for errors and tests (the IPv6 version of the ICMP from Routing, ICMP and traceroute), carried inside ordinary IPv6 packets. ARP was a protocol of its own.

And the question doesn't go to every card. It goes to the target's solicited-node multicast group: ff02::1:ff followed by the last 24 bits of the address you're looking for. For fd00:10:6::20, that's ff02::1:ff00:20. On Ethernet, the common kind of wired network, the packet travels inside a frame, the link's own envelope. That frame goes to 33:33 plus the last 32 bits, 33:33:ff:00:00:20. That's a group MAC address (the lowest bit of 33 is 1). A card only takes it if it joined the group, so in practice only the owner's card looks at it. The answer, a Neighbor Advertisement, goes straight back to the asker alone. The result sits in a neighbor table with ARP's states: REACHABLE, STALE and PROBE.

Step through it, then do it. Docker hands out IPv6 addresses itself and sends no router advertisements. So in the Try it, api plays the router, with a short Python script.

That's also the weak spot of SLAAC. Any machine on the link can send a router advertisement, and every machine believes it. One badly set-up laptop can announce itself as everyone's default router. Here the street-sign picture breaks: on a real street, people would notice a stranger putting up fake signs. Office and data-centre switches, the boxes that join the machines of one link, block advertisements from ports that shouldn't send them. That feature is called RA Guard (RFC 6105).

Now app has three addresses, and api has an IPv4 and an IPv6 one. Next, we'll see what a program does when one name leads to both.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 680 332" role="img" aria-label="app on the left and api, playing the router, on the right, the message on the link between them, and app's addresses and routes below"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="200" height="56" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="120" y="42" text-anchor="middle">app</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="120" y="62" text-anchor="middle">MAC 12:fc:01:3b:eb:52</text><rect class="box-a" x="440" y="20" width="220" height="56" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="550" y="42" text-anchor="middle">api, playing the router</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="550" y="62" text-anchor="middle">fe80::e8cd:e9ff:fe43:37ae</text><line class="ln" x1="220" y1="48" x2="440" y2="48"/><line class="ln-a" x1="520" y1="90" x2="150" y2="90" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box-a" x="90" y="102" width="500" height="78" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="340" y="126" text-anchor="middle">Router Advertisement (ICMPv6 type 134), hop limit 255</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="340" y="144" text-anchor="middle">prefix 2001:db8:6::/64, flags on-link and autonomous</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="340" y="162" text-anchor="middle">router lifetime 1800 s, to ff02::1</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="196" width="640" height="122" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-m" x="36" y="216" text-anchor="start">app's addresses and routes</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="36" y="242" text-anchor="start">fe80::10fc:1ff:fe3b:eb52/64  scope link</text></svg>
frames.say: The router answers every machine at once (ff02::1): this /64 is on this link, and the autonomous flag means "build your own address in it". It also offers itself as the default router for 1,800 seconds. Machines accept an advertisement only with hop limit 255. The hop limit is IPv6's name for the TTL, and any router would have lowered it, so 255 proves the message never left this link.

frames.say: No answer, so app now has a global address, and a default route through the router's link-local address. Nobody wrote anything down: the router keeps no list of which machine took which address. That's the stateless in SLAAC.

frames.say: Later, app wants to ping fd00:10:6::20. This is ARP's job in IPv6, and it's the same message as duplicate address detection, now with a real source. It goes to the target's solicited-node group, ff02::1:ff plus the last 24 bits of the target. On Ethernet, that's 33:33 plus the last 32 bits, a group MAC that only api's card listens to.

frames.say: api answers straight to app's MAC, and app keeps the answer in its neighbor table, with the same states as ARP: REACHABLE, then STALE. Two messages, and no broadcast anywhere in the whole sequence.

try.title: Let a machine set itself up
steps: In one terminal, listen for ICMPv6 on app with tcpdump, a tool that prints every packet a card sees: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app tcpdump -i eth0 -nn icmp6.

In a second terminal, run the router advertisement script on api. It's in labs/env/net/send-ra.py: read it first, it's short. It announces the documentation prefix 2001:db8:6::/64. Predict app's new address before you look: you know its interface ID from the last Try it.
Wait two seconds, stop tcpdump with Ctrl-C, and print app's addresses and routes.

code.title: second terminal, in labs/
code.html: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec api python3 /labs/env/net/send-ra.py 2001:db8:6::/64 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app ip -6 addr show eth0 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app ip -6 route

try.expect:
tcpdump on app, from one run:

19:04:17.938607 IP6 fe80::e8cd:e9ff:fe43:37ae > ff02::1: ICMP6, router advertisement, length 48
19:04:18.928945 IP6 :: > ff02::1:ff3b:eb52: ICMP6, neighbor solicitation, who has 2001:db8:6:0:10fc:1ff:fe3b:eb52, length 32
19:04:18.928990 IP6 :: > ff02::1:ff3b:eb52: ICMP6, neighbor solicitation, who has 2001:db8:6:0:10fc:1ff:fe3b:eb52, length 32
19:04:18.929004 IP6 :: > ff02::1:ff43:37ae: ICMP6, neighbor solicitation, who has 2001:db8:6:0:e8cd:e9ff:fe43:37ae, length 32

Then the addresses and routes (the first line and the lifetimes trimmed):

    inet6 2001:db8:6:0:10fc:1ff:fe3b:eb52/64 scope global dynamic mngtmpaddr
    inet6 fd00:10:6::10/64 scope global nodad
    inet6 fe80::10fc:1ff:fe3b:eb52/64 scope link
2001:db8:6::/64 dev eth0 proto kernel metric 256 expires 86395sec pref medium
fd00:10:6::/64 dev eth0 proto kernel metric 256 pref medium
fe80::/64 dev eth0 proto kernel metric 256 pref medium
default via fd00:10:6::1 dev eth0 metric 1024 pref medium
default via fe80::e8cd:e9ff:fe43:37ae dev eth0 proto ra metric 1024 expires 1795sec hoplimit 64 pref medium

One advertisement, and app built 2001:db8:6:0:10fc:1ff:fe3b:eb52 from the prefix plus its own interface ID. It checked the address from :: up to a second later, a random delay the RFC asks for, and added a default route through api's link-local address (proto ra). The expires values show that the new route and prefix have lifetimes: they vanish unless the router keeps advertising. You see app's check twice because the Docker bridge, the switch that joins the containers, sends multicast back out of the port it came from (hairpin mode, from The link layer: Ethernet, MAC addresses and ARP). The last line is api checking an address of its own. The bridge sent api its own advertisement back, and api believed it. Any machine that hears an advertisement takes it seriously.

sections.h: One name, two addresses: racing IPv6 against IPv4
sections.html:
Our machine api has two addresses, 10.10.6.20 and fd00:10:6::20, and one name. Running both versions side by side like this is called dual stack, and many networks now do it. Programs rarely use raw addresses. They use names such as api, and DNS, the internet's directory, turns a name into addresses. In a dual-stack world a name has an A record for its IPv4 address and an AAAA record for its IPv6 address. A program that asks for both gets two answers. Which one should it connect to?

The simplest program tries the first address and, if that fails, the next. The operating system sorts the list so that IPv6 usually comes first (RFC 6724). That works until the IPv6 path is broken. A firewall, a filter that drops some traffic on purpose, drops it, or a home router has a half-working IPv6 setup. Then every connection waits for the IPv6 attempt to time out before it tries IPv4. TCP is how programs open a lasting, reliable connection, and with Linux's default settings a TCP connection attempt gives up after about two minutes. That's a long time to stare at a spinning wheel.

Happy Eyeballs (RFC 8305) races the two instead. Start the IPv6 connection. If it hasn't connected within a short delay, 250 ms being the recommended one, start an IPv4 attempt as well. Use whichever connects first, and close the other. The user waits at most the delay, not the whole timeout. curl, the command-line tool for fetching web addresses, gives IPv6 a 200 ms head start, and the Chrome and Firefox browsers give it 300 ms.

Java does none of this, and it has its own order. Java and Kotlin programs run on the JVM, the Java Virtual Machine. The JVM's InetAddress.getAllByName returns IPv4 addresses first by default (java.net.preferIPv6Addresses=false), the opposite of the operating system. Set the property to true and IPv6 comes first, or to system to keep the operating system's order.

Either way, new InetSocketAddress(host, port) keeps only the first address. Socket.connect and HttpClient, the web client in the JDK (Java's standard toolkit), try only that one. In the Try it, with api's IPv6 port blocked, curl connects over IPv4 after 0.2 s. A JVM that prefers IPv6 waits out its whole 3-second connect timeout, and fails. And with the default setting, the JVM never uses IPv6 at all, even when it works.

A few more things change for your code once IPv6 traffic arrives:

  • An address no longer fits in 15 characters, the size many database columns were made with (VARCHAR(15)). The longest text form is 45 characters (ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:255.255.255.255). Or store the 16 bytes as binary.
  • Put brackets around an IPv6 address in a URL (a web address) or a host:port setting: http://[fd00:10:6::20]:8080/. Code that splits host:port at a colon breaks.
  • A server that listens on ::, which means every IPv6 address of the machine, accepts IPv4 clients too. Many programs then show them as IPv4-mapped addresses, an IPv4 address written inside an IPv6 one, such as ::ffff:10.10.6.10, and Python's web server in the Try it logs exactly that. The JVM turns them back into IPv4 addresses, but your logs and other tools may not.
  • Count and block clients by /64, not by single address. One IPv6 machine may legally use any of the 2^64 addresses in its network, so a limit per address is a limit on nothing.
  • Without NAT, a machine's address can be reached from outside unless a firewall says otherwise. IP addresses, subnets and NAT warned that NAT is no firewall. In IPv6, the firewall has to be a real one.

Every program so far has only connected to an address. Next, we'll look at what it sends once it's there, starting with the simplest way to send anything.

try.title: Race IPv6 against IPv4, and watch the JVM not race
steps: Look up api the way most Linux programs do: getent ahosts asks the C library, the shared code most programs use to look up names. Then fetch from api over IPv4 (-4) and over IPv6 (-6), and read api's log. Predict how the IPv4 client appears in the log of a server listening on ::.

Run Dial.java on app. It prints the addresses in the JVM's order and connects the way most JVM code does: to the first address only. The lab machines have JDK 25, which can run a single Java file without a build tool (labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l05/demo/Dial.java).

Break IPv6 on api with a firewall rule that drops its port 8080 (ip6tables is the IPv6 twin of iptables, Linux's firewall tool). Predict, then run: how long does curl take now, and what does the JVM do with and without -Djava.net.preferIPv6Addresses=true? Delete the rule at the end. When you're done with the lesson, docker compose -f env/net.yml down stops everything.

code.title: in labs/
code.html: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app getent ahosts api docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app curl -s -4 http://api:8080/ docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app curl -s -6 http://api:8080/ docker compose -f env/net.yml logs --no-log-prefix api | tail -2 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app java /labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l05/demo/Dial.java api 8080 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec api ip6tables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 8080 -j DROP docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app curl -sv -o /dev/null -w 'connected after %{time_connect} s\n' http://api:8080/ 2>&1 | grep -E 'Trying|Connected|connected after' docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app java /labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l05/demo/Dial.java api 8080 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app java -Djava.net.preferIPv6Addresses=true /labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l05/demo/Dial.java api 8080 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec api ip6tables -D INPUT -p tcp --dport 8080 -j DROP

try.expect:
From one run (getent's DGRAM and RAW lines trimmed):

fd00:10:6::20   STREAM api
10.10.6.20      STREAM
hello from api
hello from api
::ffff:10.10.6.10 - - [07/Nov/2026 19:04:23] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 -
fd00:10:6::10 - - [07/Nov/2026 19:04:23] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 -
resolved  10.10.6.20
resolved  fd00:10:6:0:0:0:0:20
connected to 10.10.6.20 in 3 ms

*   Trying [fd00:10:6::20]:8080...
*   Trying 10.10.6.20:8080...
* Connected to api (10.10.6.20) port 8080
connected after 0.201147 s
resolved  10.10.6.20
resolved  fd00:10:6:0:0:0:0:20

For the same name, the C library lists IPv6 first and the JVM lists IPv4 first. The server listening on :: logs the IPv4 client as ::ffff:10.10.6.10. The JVM prints its IPv6 address in the long form, without ::. With IPv6 blocked, curl tried IPv6, started IPv4 after 200 ms and connected over IPv4: that's Happy Eyeballs. The default JVM noticed nothing, because it never tried IPv6. The JVM that prefers IPv6 waited out its whole 3-second timeout on one address and failed, although IPv4 worked.

opening:
Picture the café's list of delivery addresses. A new order arrives for "10 High Street", and the list says "10 High St.". You'd know at once that it's the same door. A program that compares the two as text says they differ.

The payments app has the same bug in a new place. It keeps a short list of machines allowed to send it refunds. A refund arrives from fd00:10:6:0:0:0:0:10, the list says fd00:10:6::10, and the app turns its own machine away. It's an easy bug to write. With the older kind of address, nearly every program prints an address the same way, so comparing text worked for years.

Routing, ICMP and traceroute followed packets with four-number IPv4 addresses, which are running out. In this lesson, we'll meet IPv6 and its 128-bit addresses, and learn the one correct way to write each one. We'll watch a machine give itself an address, and see what a program does when a name has both kinds. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a refund turned away because two spellings of one address didn't match as text. An IPv6 address is a 128-bit number with many legal spellings, and RFC 5952's form is the one to print and store.

On a Mac, run ifconfig en0 | grep inet6 (on Windows, ipconfig). Find the fe80:: address and the % after it: that's the zone, naming the card. If more addresses follow, look for secured and temporary, the stable one and the one that changes daily.

Next, we'll stop following addresses and send some data. We'll start with UDP, the simplest way for a program to send a message, and find out what it does and doesn't promise.

compare.title: Finding a neighbor's MAC address: ARP in IPv4, neighbor discovery in IPv6

a.label: IPv4: ARP
a.title: from the link layer lesson: client asks for peer
a.html:
b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42:
    Request who-has 10.10.1.20 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
3a:42:9a:52:90:f5 > b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42:
    Reply 10.10.1.20 is-at 3a:42:9a:52:90:f5, length 28

b.label: IPv6: neighbor discovery
b.title: this lesson: app asks for api
b.html:
12:fc:01:3b:eb:52 > 33:33:ff:00:00:20, ethertype IPv6 (0x86dd), length 86:
    fd00:10:6::10 > ff02::1:ff00:20: ICMP6, neighbor solicitation, who has fd00:10:6::20, length 32
ea:cd:e9:43:37:ae > 12:fc:01:3b:eb:52, ethertype IPv6 (0x86dd), length 86:
    fd00:10:6::20 > fd00:10:6::10: ICMP6, neighbor advertisement, tgt is fd00:10:6::20, length 32

compare.note: The question and the answer are the same, and so is the reply that goes back to the asker alone. What differs is where the question goes and what carries it. ARP is its own protocol, straight on Ethernet (EtherType 0x0806, the field that says what a frame carries), and it asks every card on the link through the broadcast MAC address. Neighbor discovery is ICMPv6 inside an ordinary IPv6 packet, so it has real IPv6 addresses. It asks only the multicast group made from the target's last 24 bits, and every other card drops the frame in hardware without waking its kernel.

worked.title: From a MAC address to a canonical IPv6 address, by hand

steps.say: app's card has the MAC address 12:fc:01:3b:eb:52. Modified EUI-64 turns its 48 bits into a 64-bit interface ID. First flip the U/L bit, the 0x02 bit of the first byte, which is the second bit from the right in binary.
Then put ff:fe between the third and the fourth byte, and read the eight bytes as four 16-bit groups.
Put the link-local prefix fe80::/64 in front, which is fe80 followed by three zero groups, and write all eight groups in full.
Now apply RFC 5952. Drop the leading zeros in every group, then replace the longest run of two or more zero groups with ::. Here there's only one run, three groups long.
steps.code:
fe80:0:0:0:10fc:1ff:fe3b:eb52     no leading zeros
fe80::10fc:1ff:fe3b:eb52          the run of three zeros becomes ::

steps.say: Two cases catch people. When two runs are equally long, the first one gets ::. A single zero group never does. The lab's tests check both.

lab.title: An IPv6 address parser and formatter
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All 14 fail for now. An Ipv6 is eight 16-bit groups, and toBytes, exploded and fromBytes are finished.

Write parse. Split the text at :: (at most two halves), parse each half's groups, and fill the gap with zero groups until there are eight. A four-number IPv4 tail, as in ::ffff:10.10.6.10, counts as two groups.

Write format, the RFC 5952 form. Find the longest run of two or more zero groups (a later run must be strictly longer to win), print the groups before and after it in lower-case hex, and join them with ::. Handle IPv4-mapped addresses first.
Write kind from the prefixes on Ipv6Kind, then fromMac (modified EUI-64) and solicitedNode.

One test parses a real Neighbor Solicitation captured on app, and checks that its destination is the solicited-node address of its target. Another feeds format what Java's InetAddress.getHostAddress() returns. Run the tests until all 14 pass.
hints: "fd00:10:6".split(':') gives three groups, and an empty half (as in ::1) gives none. Without ::, you need exactly eight groups.
Int.toString(16) already drops leading zeros and prints lower case.
For format, walk the groups once. Keep track of the start and length of the current zero run and of the best run so far. If the best run is shorter than 2, join all eight groups.
Link-local is groups[0] and 0xffc0 == 0xfe80, and unique local is groups[0] and 0xfe00 == 0xfc00.

drill.title: Shorten and sort
drill.prompt: No tools. Write each address in RFC 5952 form, and name its kind (link-local, unique local, global, loopback, IPv4-mapped, multicast). Then answer: which MAC address produced the first one? (a) FE80:0000:0000:0000:0202:B3FF:FE1E:8329 (b) 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329 (c) 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1 (d) fd12:3456:789a:0001:0000:0000:0000:0000 (e) 2001:db8:0:0:1:0:0:1 (f) 0:0:0:0:0:ffff:c0a8:0101 (g) ff02:0:0:0:0:1:ff00:20

answer.html:
(a) fe80::202:b3ff:fe1e:8329        link-local
(b) 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329          global (documentation prefix)
(c) ::1                             loopback
(d) fd12:3456:789a:1::              unique local
(e) 2001:db8::1:0:0:1               global (tie: the first run gets ::)
(f) ::ffff:192.168.1.1              IPv4-mapped (c0a8 = 192.168, 0101 = 1.1)
(g) ff02::1:ff00:20                 multicast: the solicited-node group for ...:20

MAC behind (a): interface ID 0202:b3ff:fe1e:8329
  remove ff:fe        -> 02 02 b3 | 1e 83 29
  flip the U/L bit    -> 02 xor 02 = 00
  MAC 00:02:b3:1e:83:29 (a vendor-assigned card)

recap: An IPv6 address is 128 bits, written as eight groups of hex. Leading zeros may go, and one run of zero groups may become ::. RFC 5952 picks one spelling: lower case, :: for the longest run, the first run on a tie, and never for a single group.

A card has several addresses at once: a link-local fe80:: one it makes itself, plus unique local (fd00::/8) or global ones. A link-local address needs a zone, such as %eth0, to say which link it's on.
SLAAC: a router advertises a /64, and each machine adds its own 64-bit interface ID and checks the address with duplicate address detection. The router keeps no list.
Neighbor discovery replaces ARP with ICMPv6 messages sent to the target's solicited-node group (ff02::1:ff plus its last 24 bits), so there's no broadcast at all.
Happy Eyeballs gives IPv6 a 250 ms head start, then races IPv4. The JVM doesn't race: it puts IPv4 first by default and connects to the first address only.

The limit: SLAAC believes any machine that sends a router advertisement, and dual stack means two paths that can break separately. And none of it promises that data arrives. That's the job of the protocols that ride on IP, starting with UDP.

explain.prompt: A friend asks how a laptop on a fresh IPv6 network gets an address when no server hands one out. Explain it step by step, and say what replaces ARP, IPv4's way of finding a neighbor's hardware address, afterwards.
explain.answer: As soon as the network card comes up, the laptop makes a link-local address by itself: fe80:: plus a 64-bit interface ID, either built from the card's hardware address (flip one bit, put ff:fe in the middle) or random. Before using it, it sends a Neighbor Solicitation from :: asking whether anyone already has that address, and if nobody answers, it keeps it. Then it asks the routers on the link with a Router Solicitation, and a router answers with a Router Advertisement: here's the /64 prefix for this link, you may build your own address in it, and you can use me as your default router. The laptop puts its interface ID behind that prefix, checks the new address the same way, and adds a default route through the router's link-local address. The router keeps no record of it. To reach a neighbor later, the laptop sends a Neighbor Solicitation to the target's solicited-node multicast group, made from the last 24 bits of the target's address, and the owner answers with a Neighbor Advertisement sent straight back. That replaces ARP, and there's no broadcast anywhere.

deeper.html:
The IPv6 header. It's a fixed 40 bytes: the version, a traffic class, a 20-bit flow label, the payload length, the next header (the IPv4 protocol field under a new name, 58 for ICMPv6), the hop limit (the TTL under a new name), and the two addresses. There's no header checksum, because the link and the transport already check for damage, so routers don't have to work out a new one at every hop. Options moved into extension headers that sit between the IPv6 header and the payload, chained by their next-header fields.

No fragmentation in routers. An IPv6 router never cuts a packet into pieces. It drops it and sends ICMPv6 Packet Too Big (type 2), the twin of the Fragmentation Needed message from Routing, ICMP and traceroute, and only the sender may cut packets up. Every IPv6 link must carry at least 1,280 bytes (RFC 8200), so a sender that stays at or below that never needs path MTU discovery. Blocking ICMPv6 type 2 breaks IPv6 even more reliably than blocking ICMP type 3 code 4 breaks IPv4.

DHCPv6 and the flags. An advertisement carries two flags that this lesson's script leaves off. M (managed) tells machines to get their addresses from DHCPv6, and O (other) tells them to get only other settings from it, such as which DNS servers to use. DNS servers can also ride in the advertisement itself (RFC 8106). Android phones don't take addresses from DHCPv6, so networks that phones must join keep SLAAC on.

IPv6-only networks. Many mobile networks give phones only an IPv6 address. To reach servers that have only IPv4, the provider runs NAT64: a DNS64 server invents AAAA records inside 64:ff9b::/96 that carry the IPv4 address in their last 32 bits, and a gateway translates between the two versions. That's one reason an IPv6 phone can reach an IPv4-only server, and why logs may show an address nobody configured.
